e.t: This word is an interjection expressing a sudden reaction such as “ah” or “alas!” It can voice distress, grief, surprise, or strong feeling rather than name an object or describe an action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it appears 390 times, so its exact force depends on the surrounding sentence and situation. The word is used across many books, including Jeremiah, 1 Kings, Isaiah, and Exodus, showing that it serves as a recurring emotional cry in biblical speech and writing.

This Greek LXX verb means “do good to”: it describes acting beneficially toward someone or bringing good about. It is an action word, so it focuses on what a person does rather than merely on an inward desire or a general quality. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, across four verses. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains the active doing of good toward another.

“Ingloriously” means in a way that brings no glory, honor, or distinction. As an adverb, it describes how an action or event happens rather than naming a person, object, or quality. This word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 6:34. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is that something occurs without the honor or renown normally associated with a successful or notable outcome.

This adjective means “true,” describing what is truthful rather than false. It can affirm that a person, statement, report, or matter is true. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 19 times, including passages in Genesis, Deuteronomy, Nehemiah, Job, Wisdom, Isaiah, Proverbs, and 3 Maccabees. Its central idea is truthfulness: something corresponds to what is real and can be affirmed as true. The precise emphasis in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This word means “meal,” referring to ground grain prepared as food. It is a noun used for a food item rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, each in a narrative setting involving provisions or food. The word’s basic sense remains focused and practical: meal as something prepared for eating. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and the food being described there.

Alōnam, also rendered Alonam, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Ezra 8:16, identifying a particular person. Because it functions as a personal name, its significance comes from the individual it identifies and the surrounding passage, not from a general definition that applies across many verses.

This adjective describes something that cannot be measured or whose extent has no known limit. It can refer to size, quantity, distance, or greatness beyond ordinary human calculation. The central idea is not merely that a measurement was omitted, but that the thing is without a measurable boundary. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings, this word occurs seven times, including once in Isaiah and six times in deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the noun or situation it describes.

Anachereth, also rendered Anakhereth, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named entity in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Joshua 19:19. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise referent in that passage cannot be described further; the secure meaning is the personal or place-name itself, preserved as Anachereth or Anakhereth.

This word means “man” or “husband.” It normally refers to a male person, and it can specifically describe a married man in relation to his wife. The distinction comes from the sentence and surrounding passage: the same word can identify a man generally or a husband within marriage. In the Greek LXX, it occurs 1,580 times, showing broad use across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its first listed occurrence is Genesis 2:23, and its last is Song of Songs 8:11.

This verb means to “disown” or “refuse”—to reject someone or something rather than acknowledge or accept it. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Isaiah 31:7, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic sense describes an active refusal or repudiation, not merely uncertainty or neglect. The word therefore expresses a deliberate turning away from what one previously recognized, followed, possessed, or accepted.

This verb means “send away from home.” It describes moving people away from their homeland or established dwelling. As a verb, it expresses an action performed by someone rather than a person or place. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs 33 times, showing repeated use for acts of sending people away. The surrounding passage determines who is sent and why. It appears in both Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books within this Greek corpus.

This verb means to draw something or someone out from a place or position. It describes the action of bringing something outward or separating it from where it was. The central idea is movement away from an existing location or attachment, while the surrounding sentence determines exactly what is being drawn out. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs nine times, showing repeated use for this basic action rather than a rare or specialized term.

This LXX Greek verb means “architect”: it describes the work of designing or planning a structure. As a verb, it presents architecting as an action rather than naming the person who performs it. It occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, all in Exodus, so its use is focused rather than widespread. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage.

This noun means “unsoundness,” describing a condition that is not sound, whole, or healthy. It names a deficiency or damaged condition rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented in this LXX corpus, it occurs twice: once in Proverbs and once in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains a lack of soundness or integrity.

Attan is a proper name, referring to a person named Attan rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 6:44. The available lexical information gives “Attan” as the name itself and does not provide an additional translated meaning. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person’s place in the genealogy, which are not included here.

This verb means to withhold—to keep something back instead of giving or releasing it. It describes an action of refusing or failing to provide what might otherwise be given. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice, once in Nehemiah and once in Sirach. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains holding something back. The word is therefore about an act or decision concerning what is given, shared, or released.

Baitharaba, also rendered Vetharava, is a proper name for a place mentioned in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs three times, all in Joshua, in passages that name locations. The word itself functions as a place-name rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. Its exact geographic significance must be understood from the surrounding Joshua passages, since the name alone supplies the designation rather than a broader definition.

Balaan, also rendered Valaan, is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, in three verses: once in Genesis and three times in 1 Chronicles. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not establish the person’s role or significance in each passage. Its meaning here is therefore the person’s name, Balaan or Valaan.

This verb means to weigh down or depress, describing something that places a heavy burden on a person or brings them into a lowered, discouraged condition. It is a Greek LXX word found once, in Exodus 7:14. Its basic sense is physical or figurative heaviness: something can press upon someone, hinder them, or leave them dispirited. The exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on being burdened or brought low.

This word means “offspring” or “offshoot,” referring to something that comes forth from a living source. It is a noun, so it names the resulting child, growth, or branch rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 50:12. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains something produced or springing from another source.

Bougaios, also rendered Vuyeos, is a proper name used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general description, action, or quality, but a personal designation. This name occurs three times in the Greek text of Esther, appearing in Esther 1:1, 3:1, and 9:10. Because the lexical wording gives the name rather than an explanatory definition, its meaning is chiefly its identifying function: it names Bougaios or Vuyeos.

gl: part covered by the beard; chin
d: part covered by the beard; chin

e.t: This noun refers to the chin, the part of the face covered by the beard. It names a physical part of the body rather than an action or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 4 Maccabees. Its basic meaning remains the same whether the translation presents the body part as a chin or speaks of beards. The surrounding verse determines how the reference functions in each passage.

Gōnath is a proper name, rendered “Gonath,” referring to a person named in the Greek Old Testament tradition. It is not presented here as a descriptive word with an ordinary action, quality, or object meaning; its role is to identify someone. In this LXX corpus, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Kings 16:21–22. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain the person’s specific role in that passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “take.” It expresses the act of taking something or someone, with the surrounding sentence determining what is being taken and how the action functions. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, in Esther, 2 Maccabees, and 3 Maccabees. Its basic meaning remains the action of taking; the particular force in any passage must be understood from that passage’s wording and context.

This noun means an “interval”: a space or separation between things. It can describe a measurable gap or intervening space rather than an object itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 15 times, with many occurrences in descriptions of buildings and their structural spaces. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being separated or measured there.

This word describes someone who is educated or taught—someone who has received instruction. It can function as an adjective describing a person or thing as taught, and it can also be used as a noun for one who has been instructed. In the LXX corpus, it occurs twice, so its basic sense is clear, though its particular force depends on the sentence where it appears. One occurrence is rendered “taught,” matching the central idea of receiving instruction. The word does not by itself specify what was taught; the surrounding passage supplies that detail.

This Greek word means “set” or “sink,” especially describing something going down or disappearing below the horizon or surface. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming an object. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings, it occurs 24 times, covering ordinary references to something sinking as well as the setting of the sun or another heavenly body. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on downward movement, coming to rest, or the end of visible light.

Ebia, also rendered Evia, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person or family name in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Nehemiah 7:63. Because the available wording gives only the name itself and no additional definition, its central meaning is its identifying function: it names someone called Ebia or Evia.

This Greek LXX verb means “indignant.” It describes a person who reacts with strong displeasure, expressing a resentful response rather than a neutral feeling. Because it is a verb, it presents indignation as something someone experiences or expresses in a sentence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Genesis and once in Psalms. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This word means “there,” pointing to a particular place or location. It functions as an adverb, so it tells where something is or where an action is directed rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, at Job 39:29. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains a simple reference to a place.

This verb means “call out.” It expresses the action of calling someone or something directly, functioning as an active verb rather than a name or description. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Genesis and once in Deuteronomy. The surrounding wording determines exactly whom the speaker calls and why, but the central idea remains a direct call or summons. Its meaning is therefore straightforward: to call out to another person or group.

This adjective means “light,” describing something that is not heavy. It can serve as a straightforward description of weight or burden, while the surrounding verse determines its precise application. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, including passages in Exodus, Job, and Ezekiel. The English rendering “light” agrees with its stated meaning, but the word itself should be understood within each passage’s context.

Elious, also known as Elius, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint text represented here, it occurs nine times, all within Job, from Job 32:2 through Job 38:1. The name identifies the person referred to by that form; its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and passage.

Eliphalet is a proper name, rendered as “Eliphalet” or “Elifalet.” In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or idea. The name occurs five times, all in 1 Chronicles, across five verses. Because the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its specific family or historical context is not stated here. Its meaning as presented is therefore its role as a personal name: Eliphalet, also known as Elifalet.

This word means “festival exultation,” referring to the joyful celebration associated with a festival. It is a noun naming an expression or occasion of festive rejoicing rather than an action word. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at Judges 9:27. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise role in that occurrence must be understood from its passage, but its central idea is joyful celebration connected with a festival.

Emek is a proper name, preserved as “Emek,” rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Joshua 13:27. The available lexical information identifies it as a name but does not provide enough verse text or surrounding context to determine whether it names a person, place, or another specific entity. Its precise referent therefore belongs to the context of that passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “commend in; bless in.” It expresses blessing or commendation connected with, or spoken in relation to, someone or something. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, including several passages in Genesis concerning the blessing associated with Abraham and his descendants. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is to bless or commend within a stated relationship or setting.

This verb means to pour something in while it is molten, emphasizing the act of adding material in a melted, flowing state. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical writings represented here, it occurs twice, so its broader range cannot be established from frequent usage. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but the basic picture is deliberate pouring while the substance remains melted.

This verb means to influence others or have authority over them. It describes the exercise of power or control, whether through a recognized position or personal influence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 14 times, mostly in Ecclesiastes, and is also found in Ezra, Nehemiah, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on who is exercising authority and over whom.

This verb means “enroll on tablets; register.” It describes the act of formally recording people in a written register. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 1:18, so its normal meaning is represented by this single recorded use. The word emphasizes official enrollment or registration rather than a general mention or list. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the actual translation context.

This verb means “communicate with,” describing speaking or sharing with another person. It presents communication as an interaction between people rather than a solitary act. In the Greek text of the deuterocanonical books, it occurs twice, showing a focused but clear use. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains contact or exchange through communication.

This Greek LXX verb means “sprinkle upon”: to scatter or apply a small amount of liquid over something. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Leviticus 6:20, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated passages. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and ritual context. The word’s basic idea remains the act of sprinkling something onto a surface or person.

This Greek LXX verb means “gather together; bring in.” It describes the act of collecting people or things into one place or bringing them inside. Its basic sense is active and purposeful: something or someone is moved from separate places into a gathered group or contained space. The word occurs 39 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so it can describe gathering in varied settings without changing its central idea. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

ἔρευνα means “inquiry; search”: the act of seeking information, examining a matter, or investigating something. It is a noun, so it names the process or activity of searching rather than describing a person who searches. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice—once in Proverbs and once in Wisdom—showing the term’s use for deliberate investigation or examination. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This verb means “satisfied.” It describes a person or party reaching a state of satisfaction rather than naming an object, place, or person. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, it occurs 54 times across 53 verses, in both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its broad use means the surrounding sentence determines what has been satisfied and how that satisfaction is expressed; the word itself supplies the central idea of satisfaction.

This noun describes suppleness or versatility—the ability to adapt readily and move with ease from one situation or purpose to another. It points to flexible capability rather than rigidity. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Proverbs 14:35. Because the word appears only there and the verse text is not provided here, its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding context; its basic meaning remains the quality of being supple, adaptable, or versatile.

This noun refers to good cheer expressed through feasting—a joyful meal or celebration. It can describe the atmosphere of gladness associated with gathering and eating together, rather than merely the food itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs eight times, including in Esther and 3 Maccabees. Its precise emphasis in any particular passage depends on the surrounding context.

This verb means “express characteristically”: it describes giving expression to the distinctive traits that mark a person or thing. The focus is on making a subject’s characteristic nature recognizable, rather than merely naming or mentioning it. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 15:4. Its single occurrence indicates a specialized word, while its basic sense remains clear: it concerns expressing what is characteristic about the subject.

Ērae, also rendered Irae, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person or named individual in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek text, at Nehemiah 6:18. Because it is a name, its meaning is primarily identifying: it points to someone named Ērae rather than expressing a general concept or instruction.

Thapous, also rendered Thapus, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 2:43. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide an additional explanatory definition or verse text. Therefore, its ordinary meaning is simply the personal name Thapous/Thapus; its specific identity and role must be understood from the surrounding genealogy.

Thema is a proper name used to identify a particular person, family, or other named entity rather than to express a general idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, it appears eight times. Its precise referent must be determined from the surrounding passage, since the name itself does not describe the entity’s character, role, or significance. The English rendering preserves the name as “Thema.”

This Greek LXX noun means “harvester; reaper,” referring to a person who gathers a crop after it has grown. It identifies someone engaged in the work of harvesting rather than describing the crop itself. In the LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Bel and the Dragon 1:33. Its precise role in that passage depends on the surrounding verse context, but its ordinary meaning is a person who reaps or gathers produce.

This Greek LXX verb means “perturbed”: it describes a state of disturbance rather than naming a person, object, or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Song of Songs 5:4. Because the lexical definition is brief and the verse text is not included here, the safest understanding is simply that it marks being perturbed; the surrounding passage determines its precise force in that occurrence.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Iasiēl; Iasil.” It identifies a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general concept. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 7:13. The available lexical information establishes the name and its naming function, but does not provide enough verse text to describe the individual or draw conclusions about his role in that passage.

This verb expresses the idea “gracious.” It describes an action involving graciousness rather than naming a person, object, or quality by itself. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it occurs once, in Daniel 9:19. Because the word appears only there and no verse text is provided here, its precise force in that sentence must be understood from the surrounding passage. Its basic meaning remains gracious.

This word is a personal name, rendered “Isbaal” or “Izvaal.” It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Chronicles, at 1 Chronicles 9:39 and 1 Chronicles 24:13. Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, the name itself supplies the main meaning: it is a proper name used to identify a person. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding genealogical or historical context.

This adjective describes something bad or ugly—whether its condition, appearance, or character is viewed negatively. It is used broadly in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, occurring 363 times in this LXX corpus. Its central sense remains the presence of something undesirable, harmful, or unattractive, while the surrounding sentence determines which aspect is intended. The word appears especially often in Proverbs and Jeremiah, where such negative qualities are frequently described.

This adjective means “more finely,” describing something done or made in a finer, better, or more exact way than another. It expresses comparison rather than a standalone object or person, so its precise force depends on the surrounding sentence. In the Greek Old Testament writings represented here, it occurs three times, in Wisdom, Sirach, and Susanna. The word’s basic sense remains comparative: it points to a higher degree of fineness or quality.

gl: constancy of soul; steadfastness of spirit
d: constancy of soul; steadfastness of spirit

e.t: This noun means “constancy of soul” or “steadfastness of spirit.” It describes a firmly resolved inner character that remains steady rather than giving way. The word expresses enduring strength of spirit, not merely a passing feeling or momentary courage. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, so its exact force in its single reference depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea is spiritual constancy: a soul that remains firm.

This noun means “casting; founding,” referring to the act of casting or to the founding of something. The two ideas share a sense of bringing something into being or establishing its beginning. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 2:29. The reference identifies its only occurrence, but the verse text is not available here, so its precise use in that sentence must be determined from the surrounding passage.

In the Greek Old Testament, this noun means “cataract.” It names a thing rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs 11 times in the Greek Old Testament, in 11 verses ranging from Genesis through Malachi. Its central meaning remains consistent across those occurrences, while the surrounding passage determines which particular cataract is being mentioned. It appears in passages from Genesis, Leviticus, Deuteronomy, 2 Kings, Jeremiah, and Malachi.

Katorthōsis is a proper name rather than an ordinary descriptive word. Its meaning as a name or title cannot be stated more specifically from the available lexical information. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in 2 Chronicles 3:17 and once in Psalms 96:2. Since the surrounding verse text is not provided, those references alone cannot establish what person, place, thing, or idea the name identifies.

This word means “ladder,” a structure used for climbing from one level to another. It is a noun that names the object itself, whether singular or plural in translation. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, it occurs five times, including Genesis, Nehemiah, and 1 Maccabees. Its ordinary sense remains straightforward: a ladder or ladders, with the surrounding passage determining its particular use.

This word means “skull,” the noun naming the bony part of the head. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Judges and once in 2 Kings. Its basic meaning remains direct and concrete: it identifies a physical body part rather than an action, quality, or person. The precise force of the word in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

Lasendak, also rendered Lasenthak, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a specific place or named location in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once, in Joshua 19:48, so its ordinary lexical function is simply to designate that named place. The name itself does not supply a broader meaning apart from identifying the location.

This Greek LXX noun means “water closet; latrine”—a place used as a toilet. It names an ordinary sanitary facility rather than an action, person, or abstract idea. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in 2 Kings and once in Isaiah. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains a physical place for human waste.

This Greek LXX adverb means “greatly,” describing an action, condition, or feeling as occurring to a high degree. It intensifies what the sentence says rather than naming a person, object, or event. The word appears 18 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, including passages from Numbers, Chronicles, Nehemiah, Job, and the Maccabean books. Its exact force depends on the word or statement it modifies in each verse.

This verb means to impart something or give someone a share in it. It describes actively passing along what one has—whether a possession, benefit, knowledge, or portion—so that another person receives part of it. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, it occurs six times, showing a recurring idea of sharing or distributing rather than merely keeping something for oneself. Its exact object and emphasis depend on the surrounding verse, but the central sense remains giving something to another.

This Greek noun means “change of abode; removal”: a move from one dwelling or place to another, including being relocated. It names the act or condition of leaving one residence or location rather than describing a person who moves. In the Greek LXX, it occurs four times, all in four different verses. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains a change of dwelling or removal.

This verb means “afflicted with warts.” It describes being affected by warts, naming a physical condition rather than an action of choice or intention. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Leviticus 22:22, so its meaning is especially specific rather than a broad religious or moral concept. The word’s precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context.

Naama is a proper name, referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Kings 14:21. The name itself identifies its bearer, while the surrounding verse and passage are needed to understand that person’s role in the account. Thus, its basic meaning is simply the personal name “Naama,” not a general word with a broader definition.

This Greek LXX noun means “joyful,” describing someone or something marked by gladness. It expresses a positive, glad quality rather than naming an action or command. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Job 39:13. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and context, which are not included here; the basic lexical idea remains joyfulness. This word should therefore be understood as a description of glad character or condition.

This proper name refers to Nineveh, the named place associated with passages in Genesis, Jonah, Nahum, 2 Kings, Isaiah, and Zephaniah. It is a place-name rather than a description of a quality or action. In the Greek Old Testament, the name appears 17 times across 16 verses, with many occurrences in Jonah. The wording also appears in the forms “Nineuΐ” and “Ninei.” Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Greek LXX verb means to prompt or warn someone, expressing an active effort to urge a person toward attention or a needed response. It can describe instruction, correction, or a serious caution, depending on the sentence in which it appears. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek LXX corpus, including passages in 1 Samuel, Job, and Wisdom. Its central idea is directed counsel: someone addresses another person in order to awaken awareness and encourage a proper response.

This adjective means “inhabited,” describing a place where people live or that is occupied by residents. It identifies the condition of a dwelling, town, land, or other location rather than describing the people themselves. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times: once in Leviticus and twice in the Maccabean books. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic sense remains a place that is lived in or occupied.

This word means “donkey,” the familiar pack animal. It is a noun used for the animal itself, including donkeys used for carrying people or goods in the Greek Old Testament and related writings. The word occurs 113 times in the LXX corpus, appearing across many Old Testament books and once in Sirach. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains the animal “donkey.”

ὄρθρος is a noun meaning “dawn,” the early light or beginning of day. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies the time around daybreak, rather than an action or person. The word occurs 30 times within this Greek Old Testament corpus, so it is a recurring expression for the beginning of the day. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “old”. It describes something that has existed for a long time or belongs to an earlier period. As an adjective, it characterizes people, objects, supplies, or things associated with age rather than newness. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 22 times, including passages in Leviticus, Joshua, and 1 Samuel. Its exact emphasis may depend on the noun it describes, but the central idea remains age, former use, or established antiquity.

This Greek LXX noun means “delirium,” describing a state of confused or disordered thinking. It refers to impaired mental clarity rather than a deliberate choice or ordinary concern. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in Zechariah 12:4. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains a condition in which a person’s understanding is disturbed or confused.

This verb means “sad”: it describes being in a state of being sad or expressing that emotional condition. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings preserved in the Septuagint corpus, it appears 66 times, so it is a recurring word for being sad rather than a rare expression. Its exact force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This verb means “sit around” or “besiege,” describing people positioning themselves around a place, especially to surround it or press against it. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings, it is used for encircling locations during military action. It occurs 17 times in this LXX corpus, including passages in Deuteronomy and Joshua, and continues through 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on whether the surrounding context emphasizes remaining around a place or actively besieging it.

This Greek LXX verb means “dress” or “clothe”: it describes putting clothing on someone or covering someone with garments. It is an action word, focusing on the act of providing or placing clothing rather than on the clothing itself. The word occurs three times in the Greek LXX, in two Old Testament passages and once in Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage.
